extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation standards for filing and prosecuting petitions to revive abandoned U.S. patent applications under 37 CFR 1.137, including requirements for unintentional vs. unavoidable delay, fees, terminal disclaimers, and evidentiary showings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inordinate burden exception for treating replies under 37 CFR 1.111/1.113
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may treat a reply under 37 CFR 1.137(a)(1) (or 1.137(b)(1)) where, under the circumstances of the application, treating a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 or 1.113 would place an inordinate burden on the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplary circumstances when treating a reply under 1.111/1.113 may place an inordinate burden are where: (A) an application has been abandoned for an inordinate period of time; (B) an application file contains multiple or conflicting replies to the last Office action; and (C) the reply or replies submitted under 1.137(a)(1) (or 1.137(b)(1)) are questionable as to compliance with 1.111 or 1.113. The Office may require filing of a continuing application or RCE to meet reply requirements when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpublication request — foreign filing notice requirement and abandonment consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant who made a nonpublication request must notify the Office within forty-five days after filing any foreign (or multilateral treaty) application that requires eighteen-month publication; failure to timely notify will result in abandonment under 35 U.S.C. 122(b)(2)(B)(iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application abandoned due to failure to timely provide such a notice is subject to revival only on the basis of unintentional delay pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137(b) (not unavoidable delay). Notification of the foreign filing meets the reply requirement of 1.137(c). Filing a petition under 1.137(b) to revive will not stay any running reply periods against the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition fee requirement on filing
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 41(a)(7) requires that a petition for revival of an unintentionally abandoned application (or unintentionally delayed issue fee) be accompanied by the petition fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(m), unless filed under 35 U.S.C. 133 or 151 (unavoidable delay), in which case fee is per 1.17(l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'On filing' means the fee is required on filing the petition (not merely on grant). The Office will not refund the petition fee regardless of dismissal/denial, and will not reach the merits of any petition lacking the requisite petition fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice between 37 CFR 1.137(a) (unavoidable) and 1.137(b) (unintentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions under 1.137(b) are less burdensome (statement(s) rather than documentary showing) and evaluated under the less stringent 'unintentional delay' standard; petitions under 1.137(a) must establish 'unavoidable' delay to the satisfaction of the Commissioner and are more exacting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should consider filing under 1.137(b) where evidence for unavoidable delay is difficult to obtain. Many petitions initially filed under 1.137(a) end up granted under 1.137(b) when adequate evidence of unavoidable delay cannot be provided. 1.137(a) petitions typically require more interlocutory decisions and longer processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant duty of candor and reliance on unintentional delay statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office relies upon the applicant's duty of candor and good faith and generally accepts the statement that 'the entire delay ... was unintentional' in petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(b) without requiring further information in the vast majority of petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners are obligated under 37 CFR 10.18 to inquire into facts when providing such statements. Providing an inappropriate or false statement in a 1.137(b) petition may have adverse consequences (e.g., inequitable conduct affecting enforceability). If questions arise, the Commissioner may require additional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of what constitutes intentional delay (not unintentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action by the applicant is not 'unintentional' within 37 CFR 1.137(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of deliberate courses of action that preclude a finding of unintentional delay include: (A) applicant does not consider the claims patentable over outstanding references; (B) applicant considers allowed/ patentable claims not broad enough to justify expense; (C) applicant considers any patent not worth the expense; (D) applicant does not wish to maintain interest in obtaining the patent; (E) applicant seeks to defer patent fees and prosecution expenses. A later change of mind or change in circumstances does not render a prior deliberate abandonment 'unintentional.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary showing required for unavoidable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing of 'unavoidable' delay requires documentary evidence beyond a mere statement and is evaluated under a reasonably prudent person standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show unavoidable delay the petition should include: (1) evidence concerning procedures in place that should have avoided the error causing the delay; (2) evidence concerning the training and experience of persons responsible for the error; and (3) copies of applicable docketing records showing the error caused the delay. Decisions are case-by-case and the petitioner bears the burden of proof for 1.137(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and limits for showing unavoidable delay (docketing/address examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee clerical error (e.g., docketing error or change of correspondence address causing mail to go to old address) may support unavoidable delay only if due care and proper notification procedures were followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate showing for change-of-address-based delay requires evidence that due care was taken to notify the Office promptly and in a manner reasonably calculated to call attention. Mere inclusion of a different address on an unrelated paper, listing plural applications without proper procedure, or belated/absent notification are not proper notifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: What does not constitute unavoidable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay caused by lack of knowledge or improper application of the patent statute, rules of practice, or the MPEP does not constitute 'unavoidable' delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: failing to timely file necessary papers while awaiting allowance; failure to file papers/fees in compliance with 37 CFR 1.8 or 1.10; reliance on oral advice from USPTO employees; USPTO's failure to advise in time. Such causes have been held insufficient for unavoidable delay in case law (e.g., Haines, Vincent, Smith, Potter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three delay periods to evaluate in a petition
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three periods considered in evaluating a 37 CFR 1.137 petition: (A) the delay in reply that originally resulted in abandonment; (B) the delay in filing an initial petition under 1.137; and (C) the delay in filing a grantable petition under 1.137.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An intentional decision at any of these stages (permitting abandonment, delaying seeking revival, or delaying filing a grantable petition) precludes a finding of unintentional or unavoidable delay. The Office will consider all three periods when deciding a petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe-harbor timing guidance — 3 months and 1 year windows
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office generally will not question whether there was intentional/impermissible delay when a petition under 1.137 is filed (A) within 3 months of the date the applicant is first notified that the application is abandoned; and (B) within 1 year of the date of abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a petition is not filed within 3 months of notification, the Office may require showings as to how the delay was 'unavoidable' (for 1.137(a)) or how it was 'unintentional' (for 1.137(b)). If not filed within 1 year of abandonment, the Office will require additional information about when the applicant first became aware of abandonment and how the delay occurred despite due care/diligence; include these showings to avoid delay in merits consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party whose delay is relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant delay under 37 CFR 1.137 is that of the party having the right or authority to reply to avoid abandonment (or not reply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant assigns entire right, title, and interest to a third party and retains no legal or equitable interest, the applicant's delay is irrelevant. Where prosecution is controlled by a third party (partial assignee, licensee, employer), the third party's decision is binding on the applicant unless the contract expressly limits prosecution to a fiduciary role. Reassignments prior to the due date may change whose delay is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof allocation between 1.137(a) and 1.137(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.137(a)(3) requires a showing to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that the entire delay was unavoidable, placing the burden of proof on the applicant for 1.137(a); 1.137(b)(3) requires a statement that the entire delay was unintentional, though the Commissioner may require additional information where questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will require the applicant in every 1.137(a) petition to carry the burden of proof to establish that the delay from the due date for the reply until filing of a grantable petition was unavoidable. For 1.137(b), the Office generally accepts the unintentional statement but may require evidence to establish the delay was unintentional where questions arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer requirement for petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.137(d) requires that a petition under either 1.137(a) or 1.137(b) be accompanied by a terminal disclaimer (and fee) in specified circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimer (and fee) is required for: (A) design applications; (B) nonprovisional utility applications filed before June 8, 1995; (C) nonprovisional plant applications filed before June 8, 1995. Also required for utility/plant applications filed on or after June 8, 1995 but before May 29, 2000 where abandonment occurred (1) during appeal, (2) during interference, or (3) while under a secrecy order. Terminal disclaimer dedicates to the public a terminal part of the patent term equivalent to the period of abandonment (with specified limits for certain filing dates). The terminal disclaimer requirement cannot be excused by showing unavoidable or unintentional delay, nor does filing a terminal disclaimer substitute for meeting the delay standard. The Office will not indicate the period disclaimed in its decision granting revival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended practice and forms to expedite treatment for unintentional delay petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) to revive are advised to include the statement that 'the entire delay ... was unintentional' to expedite treatment and may use forms PTO/SB/64 or PTO/SB/64PCT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including the unintentional statement, even when also providing factual statements, speeds processing. Form PTO/SB/61 is provided for petitions for revival of unavoidably abandoned applications under 1.137(a).
